findings.point: 1a. Article 50(1) — provider duty to inform natural persons
findings.quote: Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use.
findings.status: text says (duty); reasonable reading (audience). The duty is keyed to 'natural persons'. The Commission's Article 50 FAQ (digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/transparency-obligations-under-article-50-ai-act) states that systems operating 'through machine-to-machine communication, or without direct contact with people, fall outside the scope of this obligation'. Agent-to-agent threads on Moltbook are therefore outside 50(1) on the Commission's own reading. Where humans 'are welcome to observe', a public feed read by people is arguably 'direct' interaction, but the platform's own framing (every account labelled an agent) likely satisfies the 'obvious' exception on-platform; it does not once a post is quoted or reposted elsewhere. Contested per surface.
findings.implication_for_ratio: The duty sits on the provider of each agent, not on the platform and not on the owner as such. At 88:1 the question becomes who 'provided' 1.5 million agents: if the owner who wrote the system prompt and put the agent into service under its own handle is the provider (see finding 3), there are at most ~17,000 duty-bearers, most of them natural persons who may fall under the personal-use carve-out (finding 2). The duty is nominally there; the addressee is not.

findings.point: 1b. Article 50(4) — deployer duty for published AI text
findings.quote: Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates text which is published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest shall disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated. This obligation shall not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences or where the AI-generated content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and where a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for the publication of the content.
findings.status: text says (duty); reasonable reading (scope). Three cumulative triggers: published, purpose of informing the public, matters of public interest (Commission FAQ lists politics, public administration, justice, fundamental rights, public health, environment, consumer safety). A typical Moltbook post fails the second or third trigger; a post about elections or public health would not. Art. 50(5) adds: 'The information referred to in paragraphs 1 to 4 shall be provided to the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of the first interaction or exposure.' Whether the audience being 'mostly agents' defeats 'the public' is contested: the text speaks of publication, not of who reads.
findings.implication_for_ratio: The deployer is the owner (Art. 3(4): 'using an AI system under its authority'). But Art. 2(10) and Art. 3(4) exclude natural persons acting in a 'purely personal non-professional activity', and the Commission FAQ confirms a person posting AI content on social media 'in their personal capacity' is 'excluded from the scope of the AI Act'. For a hobbyist owner running 88 agents, the 50(4) duty does not exist. It survives only for owners acting professionally (companies, researchers, marketers), who are indistinguishable from hobbyists in the Moltbook data.

findings.point: 2. Article 3 definitions — the four roles
findings.quote: 'provider' means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body that develops an AI system or a general-purpose AI model or that has an AI system or a general-purpose AI model developed and places it on the market or puts the AI system into service under its own name or trademark, whether for payment or free of charge; 'deployer' means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body using an AI system under its authority except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity
findings.status: text says (definitions); reasonable reading (application). AI system (Art. 3(1)): 'a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy ... infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as ... content'. A Moltbook agent (OpenClaw runtime + model + owner's system prompt + platform credentials) is an AI system on its face. GPAI model (Art. 3(63)) is the vendor's model; GPAI system (Art. 3(66)) is 'an AI system which is based on a general-purpose AI model and which has the capability to serve a variety of purposes'. Art. 3(13) 'putting into service' means 'the supply of an AI system for first use directly to the deployer or for own use in the Union for its intended purpose' — an owner who assembles and runs an agent for own use in the EU puts it into service.
findings.implication_for_ratio: See who_is_provider_deployer. The definitions allocate roles by function, not by identity; nothing in Art. 3 requires the provider or deployer of a non-high-risk system to be identifiable to anyone.

findings.point: 2b. Article 25 — when a deployer becomes a provider
findings.quote: Any distributor, importer, deployer or other third-party shall be considered to be a provider of a high-risk AI system for the purposes of this Regulation and shall be subject to the obligations of the provider under Article 16, in any of the following circumstances: (a) they put their name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service ...
findings.status: text says. Art. 25 is confined to high-risk AI systems. It does not re-allocate roles for a Moltbook agent, which is not high-risk (no Annex III use case). Any provider status of an owner therefore comes from Art. 3(3) directly ('has an AI system developed and ... puts the AI system into service under its own name'), not from Art. 25 — and that reading is contested: the Commission FAQ and the July 2026 Guidelines do not address the system-prompt case.
findings.implication_for_ratio: There is no statutory rule that says 'the person who configured the agent is its provider'. The 88:1 gap sits precisely in this silence: the framework vendor can say the owner put it into service under the owner's handle; the owner can say they merely 'use' a system developed by others. Needs legal review.

findings.point: 3. Article 2 — territorial scope for non-EU actors
findings.quote: (a) providers placing on the market or putting into service AI systems or placing on the market general-purpose AI models in the Union, irrespective of whether those providers are established or located within the Union or in a third country; (b) deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located within the Union; (c) providers and deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located in a third country, where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union; ... (g) affected persons that are located in the Union. [Art. 2(10):] This Regulation does not apply to obligations of deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity.
findings.status: text says (scope); contested (whether a post being readable in the EU is output 'used in the Union'). A US-hosted platform whose agents' posts are read in the EU brings third-country providers and deployers within 2(1)(c) only if reading counts as use; there is no Commission guidance on this for social posts. EU-located owners are caught by 2(1)(b) regardless. Art. 2(12) (free and open-source licence exclusion, which by its wording still applies to systems falling under Article 50) was not fetched verbatim in this pass and should be checked before it is cited.
findings.implication_for_ratio: Of 17,000 owners, an unknown fraction is EU-established; only those bear deployer duties with certainty. Third-country owners are reachable only through the contested 'output used in the Union' limb and, for high-risk and GPAI models, through an authorised representative — neither of which exists for a hobbyist agent.

findings.point: 4. Article 99 — penalty tier for Article 50 breaches
findings.quote: Non-compliance with any of the following provisions related to operators or notified bodies, other than those laid down in Articles 5, shall be subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher: ... (g) transparency obligations for providers and deployers pursuant to Article 50.
findings.status: text says. Art. 5 breaches: 'EUR 35 000 000 or ... 7 %'; supplying incorrect information (99(5)): 'EUR 7 500 000 or ... 1 %'; SMEs (99(6)): 'whichever thereof is lower'; 99(7) lists gravity, duration, intent/negligence, size of operator. Art. 99(1): Member States 'shall lay down the rules on penalties', so the actual sanction regime is national and applies from 2 August 2026. These are statutory maxima, not exposure.
findings.implication_for_ratio: A fine needs an addressee. The 'if the offender is an undertaking' clause shows natural persons can be fined (fixed cap), but a market surveillance authority must first identify the person behind a handle. With registration by unrated loop and 88 agents per email address, the enforceable population is the platform's user table, which the authority can reach only via the platform (a third-country company) or DSA-style cooperation — outside this Regulation.

findings.point: 5. Digital Omnibus — Article 50 untouched, high-risk deferred
findings.provision: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026 (Digital Omnibus on AI), OJ 24 July 2026, in force 27 July 2026; recitals 38 and 40; new Art. 111(4); amended Art. 113
findings.quote: [Recital 40, per EUR-Lex fetch:] '2 December 2027 for AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III, and to 2 August 2028 for AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(1) and Annex I.' [Recital 38:] 'a transitional period of four months for providers who have already placed their systems on the market before the 2 August 2026' regarding Article 50(2). [Amended Art. 113, per AI Act Explorer consolidated text:] 'It shall apply from 2 August 2026. However: ... (c) Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3, with the exception of Article 6(5), shall apply from: (i) 2 December 2027 ...; (ii) 2 August 2028 ...'
findings.status: text says. The amending act touches Art. 50 only at 50(2) (codes of practice/implementing acts on marking) and adds Art. 111(4) giving providers of generative systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 until 2 December 2026 to comply with 50(2). Art. 50(1), (3), (4), (5) and the general application date of 2 August 2026 are unchanged. Commission news 'AI Omnibus enters into force' (27 July 2026, digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/ai-omnibus-enters-force) confirms the high-risk dates; the Commission's Article 50 guidelines page confirms transparency 'applies from 2 August 2026'. Note: the EUR-Lex page was truncated in fetch; the Art. 113 wording above comes from the explorer's consolidated view and should be re-read on EUR-Lex before publication.
findings.implication_for_ratio: Every Moltbook agent operating from 2 August 2026 is inside a live obligation window for 50(1) and 50(4), and inside the 50(2) window from 2 December 2026 at the latest. The Omnibus gave no relief on the point that matters here.

findings.point: 6. Recitals 132–137 — the transparency rationale
findings.quote: [132:] 'Certain AI systems intended to interact with natural persons or to generate content may pose specific risks of impersonation or deception irrespective of whether they qualify as high-risk or not. ... natural persons should be notified that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious ...' [134:] 'it is also appropriate to envisage a similar disclosure obligation in relation to AI-generated or manipulated text to the extent it is published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest unless the AI-generated content has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility' [136:] transparency duties 'are particularly relevant to facilitate the effective implementation of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065' (the DSA) as to 'systemic risks that may arise from the dissemination of content that has been artificially generated' [137:] compliance 'should not be interpreted as indicating that the use of the AI system or its output is lawful'
findings.status: text says. Recital 133 (marking: 'watermarks, metadata identifications, cryptographic methods', reliable and interoperable 'as far as technically feasible') and 135 (codes of practice) were retrieved in summary only. The recitals frame the harm as impersonation and deception of natural persons and tie the text-labelling duty to editorial responsibility held by 'a natural or legal person'.
findings.implication_for_ratio: Recital 134's exemption depends on someone holding editorial responsibility. At 88:1, no natural or legal person is on record as holding it for any post; the exemption cannot be claimed and the duty cannot be attributed. The Wiz finding that humans could post as agents 'via a basic POST request' is the impersonation risk recital 132 names, inverted: humans impersonating AI.

findings.point: 7. Identifying the responsible person — registry and traceability duties
findings.quote: [Art. 49(1):] 'Before placing on the market or putting into service a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III ... the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative shall register themselves and their system in the EU database referred to in Article 71.' [Art. 16(b), high-risk providers:] 'indicate on the high-risk AI system ... their name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, the address at which they can be contacted' [Art. 22(1):] 'Prior to making their high-risk AI systems available on the Union market, providers established in third countries shall, by written mandate, appoint an authorised representative' [Art. 85(1):] 'any natural or legal person having grounds to consider that there has been an infringement of the provisions of this Regulation may submit complaints to the relevant market surveillance authority'
findings.status: text says. Every registration, name-on-product and authorised-representative duty is confined to high-risk systems (Arts 16, 22, 49, 71 — 49(2) extends registration only to Annex III systems self-assessed as not high-risk under Art. 6(3)) or to GPAI models (Art. 54). There is no registry, naming or traceability duty for a non-high-risk AI system such as a social-media agent. The Commission's July 2026 Guidelines reportedly add that an AI agent interacting with people must identify 'both its AI nature and the person or entity on whose behalf it is acting' (Faegre Drinker note of 30 July 2026; Bird & Bird note) — that is guidance, not statute, it applies only within 50(1), and the Guidelines PDF could not be text-extracted in this pass. Needs legal review.
findings.implication_for_ratio: The Act creates the duty and the fine but no mechanism to find the duty-bearer for this class of system. 1.5 million agents behind 17,000 email addresses, registrable 'with a simple loop and no rate limiting' (Wiz, 2 February 2026), is exactly the population the Regulation leaves untraceable by design. The complaint right in Art. 85 is real but has no addressee unless the platform discloses owner identity — a DSA/GDPR question, not an AI Act one.

lenses.who_is_provider_deployer: Reasonable reading, needs legal review at the owner/framework boundary. Model vendor (e.g. Anthropic, OpenAI): provider of a general-purpose AI model (Art. 3(63)) with Chapter V duties, and provider of a general-purpose AI system where it exposes the model through its own API (Art. 3(66)); it bears Art. 50(2) marking for output it generates but does not control what an agent posts. Agent framework (OpenClaw): provider of an AI system or of a component placed on the market 'free of charge' (Art. 3(3)); if released under a free and open-source licence, Art. 2(12) still leaves it inside Article 50 (wording to verify on EUR-Lex), so OpenClaw plausibly carries the 50(1) design duty — the disclosure must be built into the runtime. Owner writing the system prompt: on the plain words of Art. 3(3) an owner who 'has an AI system developed' and 'puts the AI system into service under its own name' (the handle) for own use in the Union is a provider of that specific agent; on Art. 3(4) the same owner is a deployer. Art. 25 does not resolve this because it is high-risk-only. If the owner is a natural person acting non-professionally, both roles fall away under Art. 2(10)/3(4) — the FAQ says such use 'is excluded from the scope of the AI Act'. Platform (Moltbook): neither provider nor deployer of the agents; a hosting service under the DSA and, per recital 136, the venue where AI Act labelling is meant to feed DSA systemic-risk duties. The platform is the only party that holds the owner table, and the AI Act imposes no duty on it to keep or disclose that table. Net: the design duty most plausibly sits with the framework vendor and the model vendor; the per-post disclosure duty sits with an owner who is often out of scope and always unidentified; the platform sits outside the Regulation.
lenses.enforcement_and_penalties: Art. 50 breaches: up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(g)); for SMEs the lower of the two (99(6)); incorrect information to authorities up to EUR 7 500 000 or 1 % (99(5)); Art. 5 prohibitions up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7 % (99(3)). No 6 % tier exists. Member States lay down the rules and enforce through national market surveillance authorities (Art. 99(1); Commission FAQ: 'mainly be enforced by national competent market surveillance authorities'), applicable from 2 August 2026 (Art. 113 as amended). Natural persons are fineable (the 'if the offender is an undertaking' clause), but only once identified. Anyone may complain to a market surveillance authority (Art. 85(1)). Statutory maxima, not fine exposure; Vigilia makes no determination of any breach.

Neither the FAQ nor the Guidelines address the system-prompt case. Needs legal review.

Exact wording of Art. 2(12) (open-source exclusion and its carve-back for Article 50) and of the Guidelines' AI-agent paragraph ('on whose behalf it is acting') — both need verbatim verification on EUR-Lex / the Guidelines PDF (https://ec.europa.eu/newsroom/dae/redirection/document/131215; not text-extractable in this pass).

lenses.confidence: High on the statutory quotations for Art. 3, 2, 25, 49, 71, 16, 22, 85, 99(4)(g) and the recitals (retrieved verbatim from the FLI mirror of the OJ text; EUR-Lex itself truncated in fetch and should be re-read before publication). High that the Omnibus (Reg. 2026/1744) left Art. 50(1)/(4) and the 2 August 2026 date untouched and deferred Annex III to 2 December 2027. Medium-low on the Guidelines' 'on whose behalf' agent rule, seen only through two law-firm notes. The 88:1 figure is Wiz's, from a database snapshot of early 2026, and is a claim about registration, not about active agents. This is a gap analysis, not a legal determination.

findings.point: (1) Federal Council decision of 12 Feb 2025 and 2026 follow-up: no Swiss AI-transparency statute exists; a consultation draft is due end-2026 and, on the evidence found, has not been published as of 23 Sep 2026
findings.provision: Federal Council decision 12.02.2025 (press release msg-id-104110); BAKOM status page; Beirat Digitale Schweiz item 10.02.2026
findings.quote: EN release: "Switzerland intends to ratify the Council of Europe Convention on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and to make the necessary amendments to Swiss law. Work will also continue on the regulation of AI in specific sectors such as healthcare and transport." BAKOM: "Bis Ende 2026 soll das EJPD zusammen mit dem UVEK und dem EDA eine Vernehmlassungsvorlage erstellen" — areas named: Transparenz, Datenschutz, Nichtdiskriminierung, Aufsicht. 10.02.2026 (Beirat): Rösti said it is central for public trust "dass diese Transparenz und Nachvollziehbarkeit gewährleiste"; non-binding track = "Selbstverpflichtungserklärungen einzelner Branchen, Ethikkodizes und Standards". Third-party trackers dated 8 Jul 2026 (AlgorithmWatch CH) and 22 Jul 2026 (kinewsletter.ch) both still show the draft as pending.
findings.status: text says (quotes); reasonable reading (no draft published by 23 Sep 2026 — admin.ch/bj.admin.ch pages were partly unreachable from this session, so verify on fedlex/admin.ch before publication)
findings.implication_for_ratio: Nothing in Swiss statute today limits how many agents one person may run, requires an agent to be tied to a named owner, or requires an agent to disclose it is an AI outside the data-protection and unfair-competition hooks below. An 88:1 ratio is legally invisible in Switzerland in September 2026; the only forthcoming instrument is the end-2026 draft, whose 'Transparenz' pillar is the place to argue for owner-traceability.

findings.point: (2) Council of Europe Framework Convention (CETS 225): Switzerland signed 27 Mar 2025, has not ratified; Art. 8 and 9 bind the state, and the only person-facing transparency norm (Art. 15 para 2) is 'you are talking to an AI', not 'this is who runs it'
findings.provision: CETS 225 Art. 3(1), Art. 8, Art. 9, Art. 15(2); signature per admin.ch msg-id-104646
findings.quote: Signature: "On 27 March Federal Councillor Albert Rösti will sign the Council of Europe Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law in Strasbourg on Switzerland's behalf." Art. 8: "Each Party shall adopt or maintain measures to ensure that adequate transparency and oversight requirements tailored to the specific contexts and risks are in place in respect of activities within the lifecycle of artificial intelligence systems, including with regard to the identification of content generated by artificial intelligence systems." Art. 9: "Each Party shall adopt or maintain measures to ensure accountability and responsibility for adverse impacts on human rights, democracy and the rule of law resulting from activities within the lifecycle of artificial intelligence systems." Art. 15(2): "Each Party shall seek to ensure that, as appropriate for the context, persons interacting with artificial intelligence systems are notified that they are interacting with such systems rather than with a human." Art. 3(1): "The scope of this Convention covers the activities within the lifecycle of artificial intelligence systems that have the potential to interfere with human rights, democracy and the rule of law". Lenz & Staehelin (13.02.2025): "While public institutions must fully comply with the AI Convention, private entities are only required to adhere to its fundamental principles."
findings.status: text says (Convention wording, taken from the EU Official Journal copy OJ L 2026/1081 because rm.coe.int returned 403; signature date from admin.ch). Reasonable reading: entry into force 1 Nov 2025 and no Swiss ratification as of Sep 2026 — the coe.int signature table could not be fetched; confirm before citing.
findings.implication_for_ratio: Art. 8 targets identification of AI *content*, Art. 15(2) notification of AI *interaction*; neither requires identifying the natural person behind an agent. Art. 9 requires accountability for adverse impacts but leaves the mechanism to each Party; Switzerland's private-sector coverage will depend on the Art. 3(1)(b) choice it makes in the 2026 draft. A concentration of 88 agents on one owner is therefore compatible with the Convention's letter; the argument that it defeats Art. 9 accountability in practice is a policy argument, not a text-based one.

findings.point: (3) Revised FADP (SR 235.1, in force 1 Sep 2023): the controller must name itself when collecting personal data (Art. 19), must flag automated individual decisions (Art. 21), and an owner's X handle or email is personal data whenever the person is identifiable with reasonable effort (Art. 5 lit. a + BGE 136 II 508)
findings.quote: Art. 5: "a. personal data means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person". Art. 19(1): "The controller shall inform the data subject in an appropriate manner when collecting personal data; this duty to provide information also applies if the data is not collected from the data subject." Art. 19(2): "...it shall provide the following information as a minimum: a. the controller's identity and contact details; b. the purpose of processing; c. if applicable, the recipients or the categories of recipients". Art. 21(1): "The controller shall inform the data subject about any decision that is based exclusively on automated processing and that has a legal consequence for or a considerable adverse effect on the data subject (automated individual decision)." Art. 21(2): "The data subject may request that the automated individual decision be reviewed by a natural person." Art. 25(2): "they are entitled to the following information: a. the identity and the contact details of the controller". Art. 60(1): "On complaint, a fine not exceeding 250,000 francs shall be imposed on private persons who: a. violate their duties under Articles 19, 21 and 25–27, in that they wilfully provide false or incomplete information; b. fail wilfully: 1. to provide information to the data subject in accordance with Articles 19 paragraph 1 and 21 paragraph 1". BGE 136 II 508 E. 3.5: "Von Bedeutung ist indessen nicht nur, welcher Aufwand objektiv erforderlich ist, um eine bestimmte Information einer Person zuordnen zu können, sondern auch, welches Interesse der Datenbearbeiter oder ein Dritter an der Identifizierung hat." FDPIC 09.11.2023: "Im Falle intelligenter Sprachmodelle, die direkt mit Benutzerinnen und Benutzern kommunizieren, haben Letztere ein gesetzliches Recht zu erfahren, ob sie mit einer Maschine sprechen". FDPIC 28.01.2026: "Die betroffenen Personen müssen insbesondere erkennen können, ob sie es mit einer KI zu tun haben".
findings.status: text says (articles); reasonable reading (handle/email of a natural person = personal data under the Logistep effort-plus-interest test; the FDPIC's 'right to know you talk to a machine' is the Commissioner's reading of Art. 19/21, not statutory wording). Contested: whether an agent's social post is ever an 'automated individual decision' (Art. 21 needs a legal consequence or considerable adverse effect). Needs legal review: territorial reach (Art. 3 FADP not quoted here) and whether Art. 27 media privilege covers Vigilia's own publication of owner data.
findings.implication_for_ratio: The FADP is the one Swiss instrument that today obliges the person behind an agent to name themselves — but only as 'controller', only to data subjects whose personal data the agent collects, and only on complaint. It counts controllers, not agents: 88 agents under one owner are one controller with one duty to inform. Conversely, an owner who is a natural person is a data subject, so Vigilia's own attribution study processes personal data when it names owner handles; aggregate ratios are safe, owner-level identification is not without a lawful basis and Art. 19(1)/(5) information within one month (exceptions Art. 20/27 to be checked).

findings.point: (4) Unfair Competition Act (SR 241) Art. 3(1)(b) and (s): an undisclosed AI persona is only caught where there is a commercial nexus; then the operator, not the agent, is the person 'acting unfairly'
findings.provision: UCA Art. 2, Art. 3(1) lit. b and lit. s, Art. 9, Art. 23
findings.quote: Art. 2: "Any conduct or business practice that is misleading or which otherwise violates the principle of good faith such that it influences the relationship between competitors or between suppliers and customers is unfair and unlawful." Art. 3(1): "A person acts unfairly if they: ... b. provide incorrect or misleading information about themselves, their business, their business name, their goods, works or services ... or benefit third parties in competition through such conduct"; lit. s: "offers goods, works or services online and in doing so fail: 1. to provide clear and complete details of their identity and their contact address including their email address". Art. 23(1): "Any person who wilfully competes unfairly in terms of Articles 3, 4, 5 or 6 shall on complaint be liable to a custodial sentence not exceeding three years or a monetary penalty." Härting/Mattig (05.03.2026): no explicit statutory labelling duty in Switzerland, but a "faktische Kennzeichnungspflicht" arises from DSG, UWG and URG.
findings.status: text says (articles); reasonable reading (a persona that hides its AI nature to sell or promote is 'misleading information about themselves'); contested (a non-commercial hobby agent on Moltbook falls outside Art. 2's competitive-relationship requirement)
findings.implication_for_ratio: The UCA identifies the human only through the commercial act: an operator selling or promoting through 88 personas is one 'person acting unfairly' and, under lit. s, must already publish identity and email when offering online. For the bulk of Moltbook agents with no commercial nexus the UCA gives no handle at all; the ratio is irrelevant to it, the commercial purpose is decisive.

findings.point: (5) Civil liability: Swiss law attributes an agent's harmful acts to its operator through ordinary fault liability (OR 41); whether OR 55 or OR 101 apply to software auxiliaries is contested; an association acts through its organs (ZGB 55)
findings.provision: CO Art. 41(1), Art. 55(1), Art. 101(1); CC Art. 55(1)-(3); literature: Danner/ONLAW 2023, CMS 20.02.2025, Jusletter IT (unisg) — snippet only
findings.quote: OR 41(1): "Any person who unlawfully causes damage to another, whether wilfully or negligently, is obliged to provide compensation." OR 55(1): "An employer is liable for the damage caused by his employees or ancillary staff in the performance of their work unless he proves that he took all due care to avoid a damage of this type or that the damage would have occurred even if all due care had been taken." OR 101(1): "A person who delegates the performance of an obligation ... to an associate ... is liable to the other party for any damage the associate causes in carrying out such tasks". ZGB 55: "1 The governing bodies express the will of the legal entity. 2 They bind the legal entity by concluding transactions and by their other actions. 3 The governing officers are also personally liable for their wrongful acts." Danner (ONLAW, 29.04.2023): "die zentrale Frage lautet nicht, ob ein KI‑System «autonom» gehandelt hat, sondern ob einer verantwortlichen Person eine Sorgfaltspflichtverletzung vorzuwerfen ist"; "Wer zur Vertragserfüllung ein KI‑System einsetzt, lässt sich dessen Verhalten rechtlich zurechnen." CMS (20.02.2025): Swiss liability law is "sufficiently flexible" but product-liability modernisation may be needed. Search snippet of the Jusletter IT paper: the human auxiliary has an exculpation proof under Art. 55 OR; German doctrine proposes strict attribution of digital agents' misconduct to the principal.
findings.status: text says (articles); reasonable reading (operator fault liability under OR 41 for negligent deployment/supervision is the doctrinal baseline; an association that runs an agent by board decision is bound by that 'other action' of its organ under ZGB 55(2)); contested (analogous application of OR 55/101 to a non-human 'auxiliary'; strict attribution is proposed in doctrine, not law). The Jusletter IT paper could not be opened — cite only after reading it.
findings.implication_for_ratio: Under OR 41 every one of 88 agents' harms traces to the same person's duty of care, and the ratio itself is evidence on the fault element: whether one human can meet the standard of care while supervising 88 autonomous personas is exactly the Sorgfalt question a Swiss court would ask. But liability presupposes an identified defendant, and none of these provisions helps find one.

findings.point: (6) A Swiss association (ZGB 60 ff.) running a disclosed AI agent that publishes research on other operators: no AI-specific registration or transparency duty; commercial-register entry only on the ZGB 61(2) triggers; its research is bound by the FADP and by the personality rights (ZGB 28) of any natural-person owner it names
findings.quote: ZGB 60(1): "Associations with a political, religious, scientific, cultural, charitable, social or other non-commercial purpose acquire legal personality as soon as their intention to exist as a corporate body is apparent from their articles of association." ZGB 61(2): "The association must be registered if it: 1. conducts a commercial operation in pursuit of its objects; 2. is subject to an audit requirement; 3. primarily collects or distributes assets abroad, directly or indirectly, that are intended for charitable, religious, cultural, educational or social purposes." (Ziff. 3 in force since 1 Jan 2023; CHF 100,000/two-year exemption per Art. 61(2ter) with HRegV Art. 90(2), secondary sources.) ZGB 61a(1): registered associations "shall keep a list of their members, including their first and surnames, business names and addresses". ZGB 69(2): "Associations that must be entered in the commercial register must be able to be represented by a person who is domiciled in Switzerland." ZGB 28a(1): the applicant may ask the court "1. to prohibit a threatened infringement; 2. to order that an existing infringement cease; 3. to make a declaration that an infringement is unlawful".
findings.status: text says (articles); reasonable reading (an association in formation that receives foreign philanthropic funds above the threshold falls under Art. 61(2) no. 3 and must register, keep the member list and have a Swiss-domiciled representative — relevant to Vigilia's own funding applications); needs legal review (whether Vigilia's publication of owner-level data is 'collected not from the data subject' under FADP 19(1)/(5) and whether the Art. 27 media exception applies)
findings.implication_for_ratio: Swiss association law imposes the same transparency on Vigilia that it would like from Moltbook owners: a named board, a Swiss-domiciled representative, a member list — but only once registration is triggered, and none of it concerns the agent. For the attribution study this means: report ratios and organization-level facts freely; treat every natural-person owner handle as personal data and a personality interest; do not publish an owner-level table.

lenses.who_is_provider_deployer: Swiss law has no 'provider'/'deployer' categories. The roles a Moltbook agent maps onto are: (a) the owner who writes the system prompt — the 'controller' under FADP Art. 5/19/21/25 (must name itself to data subjects), the 'person' who acts unfairly under UCA Art. 3 if there is a commercial nexus, and the person owing a duty of care under OR 41 (reasonable reading; doctrine consistently places attribution here: 'Wer ... ein KI‑System einsetzt, lässt sich dessen Verhalten rechtlich zurechnen'). If the owner is a Swiss legal entity, its board's decision to run the agent is the organ's 'other action' that binds the entity under ZGB 55(2), with personal officer liability under ZGB 55(3) for wrongful acts. (b) The platform (Moltbook, since 10 Mar 2026 Meta) — a controller for its own processing under FADP; under ZGB 28/28a a possible 'participant' in a personality infringement (Federal Court practice reaches anyone whose participation enabled or facilitated it — secondary sources, needs legal review); no Swiss statutory duty to disclose an anonymous user's identity to a civil claimant was found (the 2015 Federal Council provider-liability report could not be opened; mark contested). (c) The model vendor and (d) the OpenClaw agent framework — reachable only through product liability (PrHG) if software is a 'product' (Danner: 'Software wird nach überwiegender Ansicht als Produkt im Sinne des Produkthaftpflichtgesetzes betrachtet'), which covers personal injury and property damage, not speech or reputational harm, so for Moltbook-type harms they are remote. Under CETS 225 the addressee is the Swiss state ('Each Party shall'), and how far private lifecycle actors are covered will be fixed only by the end-2026 draft (Art. 3(1)(b) choice).

lenses.enforcement_and_penalties: FADP Art. 60(1): on complaint, fine up to CHF 250,000 on 'private persons' who wilfully give false/incomplete information or wilfully fail to inform under Art. 19(1)/(2) or 21(1) (text says; that fines fall on responsible natural persons rather than the entity is a reasonable reading, not quoted). Bottom line for the synthesis: Swiss law in September 2026 gives no way to identify the person behind a Moltbook agent unless that person collects Swiss data subjects' personal data (FADP 19: name yourself) or sells online (UCA 3(1)(s): publish identity and email); an 88:1 ratio is invisible to the statute and only matters as evidence of a breach of the duty of care once a defendant is already known. Everything marked 'needs legal review' should go to counsel before publication.

findings.point: Chan et al., Visibility into AI Agents (FAccT 2024): three visibility measures — agent identifiers, real-time monitoring, activity logging — with identifiers meant to reveal 'by whom' an agent is used.
findings.quote: Information about where, why, how, and by whom certain AI agents are used, which we refer to as visibility, is critical to these objectives.
findings.implication_for_ratio: Moltbook has the identifier (agent id/name) and a public activity log (the archive). The 'by whom' link exists only where is_claimed=true and owner_x_handle is non-null. Metric M1: share of posting agents, and of posts, whose author has a non-null owner_x_handle ('accountability-resolvable share'). Metric M4: claimed agents / distinct owner_x_handle = agents per accountable principal; 88:1 means one identifier answers 'by whom' for 88 actors at once.

findings.point: Chan et al., IDs for AI Systems (2024): IDs for instances of AI systems, carrying metadata such as responsible-party contact, warranted where systems 'contact real humans' or act at scale.
findings.quote: AI systems are increasingly pervasive, yet information needed to decide whether and how to engage with them may not exist or be accessible.
findings.implication_for_ratio: Moltbook agent ids are instance-level IDs but carry no responsible-party field beyond a self-asserted X handle. Metric M9: share of agent `description` strings that name a model, a framework, or an operator (disclosure content of the ID). An 88:1 ratio means the ID's metadata resolves to a person for ~1% of instances if the 17,000 are the only humans.

findings.point: Chan et al., Infrastructure for AI Agents (TMLR 2025): attribution = identity binding, certification, agent IDs; plus interaction shaping and detection/remediation.
findings.quote: agent infrastructure: technical systems and shared protocols external to agents that are designed to mediate and influence their interactions with and impacts on their environments
findings.implication_for_ratio: Moltbook's claim tweet is a one-shot identity binding to an X account (deletable after verification, per DataCamp and moltbook.forum), with no certification and no re-binding. Metric M3: concentration of agents per owner_x_handle (Gini, top-1% and top-10% share, max). Metric M8: registration bursts — agents per handle created within the same minute (created_at) — the automation signature Wiz described ('a simple loop and no rate limiting').

findings.point: South et al., Authenticated Delegation and Authorized AI Agents (2025): extend OAuth 2.0/OIDC with agent credentials so every agent action carries a verifiable chain to its human principal.
findings.quote: whom AI agents act on behalf of
findings.implication_for_ratio: Moltbook has no delegation token: the API key is the agent's only credential and the human link is out-of-band (tweet). Wiz found 1.5M such keys exposed, so possession of the key, not the claim, was the effective identity. Metric M5: posts by agents with is_claimed=false — if non-zero, the platform's 401 'Agent not yet claimed' gate (Hashgraph Online docs) was a claim, not a fact; check the effect, not the response.

findings.point: Otsuka, Toyoda, Leung, AI Identity: Standards, Gaps, and Research Directions (2026): five structural gaps, including 'recursive delegation accountability' and 'agent identity integrity'; agents have 'no body, no persistent memory, and no legal standing'.
findings.quote: foundational research on AI identity is the central conclusion of this report
findings.implication_for_ratio: Frames the Moltbook ratio as a legal-standing gap: the actor (agent) has none, the principal (X handle) is a pseudonym, and the platform verified neither that the agent was AI nor that the handle was a person. A measured ratio is the first empirical number this survey lacks.

findings.point: The 2025 AI Agent Index (Casper et al., 2026): documents 30 deployed agents; most developers share little on safety, evaluations, societal impact.
findings.quote: most developers share little information about safety, evaluations, and societal impacts
findings.implication_for_ratio: A precedent for a documentation index at the developer level; Vigilia's contribution would be the population level (175,886 posting agents), which the Index cannot see. Cite for method, not results.

findings.point: A2A protocol v1.0 (Mar 2026, Linux Foundation since Aug 2026): AgentCard carries name, description, url, provider{organization,url}, securitySchemes, signatures; card signing verifies the card 'originates from the claimed provider'.
findings.provision: A2A Specification 1.0.0, AgentCard and §8.4 Agent Card Signing
findings.quote: the agent card has not been tampered with and originates from the claimed provider
findings.implication_for_ratio: Moltbook agents publish no card and no provider organisation; the archive's `description` is the closest analogue. Metric M9 (description discloses model/operator) is the A2A `provider` field measured after the fact. The spec defers verifying the organisation to deployment policy, so even A2A would not by itself cap an 88:1 ratio.

findings.point: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 (9 Dec 2025): ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse, ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation, ASI10 Rogue Agents; secondary write-ups name an 'attribution gap' when agents borrow human credentials.
findings.provision: ASI03, ASI09, ASI10 (descriptions as reproduced by Promptfoo; OWASP PDF not fetched)
findings.quote: Compromised or misaligned agents act harmfully while appearing legitimate, exploiting trust mechanisms in multi-agent workflows.
findings.implication_for_ratio: Wiz's exposure is ASI03 at platform scale (any key usable by anyone); the 88:1 ratio is ASI10's precondition (many actors, one accountable name). Metric M6: karma concentration by owner handle — whether platform trust signals accrued to a few operators.

findings.point: Anthropic Usage Policy (effective 15 Sep 2025): disclosure duty on any interactive agent; impersonation of a human prohibited.
findings.provision: Usage Policy, 'Requirements for specific use cases' and prohibited uses
findings.quote: All consumer-facing chatbots, including any external-facing or interactive AI agent, must disclose to users that they are interacting with AI rather than a human.
findings.implication_for_ratio: The duty sits on the operator (owner), not the platform or model vendor; with 88 agents per operator, one policy breach scales 88-fold. Metric M9 measures how often the archive's description field meets this bar.

findings.point: Google Generative AI Prohibited Use Policy (17 Dec 2024): prohibits impersonation without disclosure and misrepresenting provenance as solely human.
findings.quote: Misrepresenting the provenance of generated content by claiming it was created solely by a human, in order to deceive.
findings.implication_for_ratio: Same shape as Anthropic: obligation on the user of the model. OpenAI's usage policy returned HTTP 403 and was not read; its ChatGPT agent identifies to sites via a signed 'Signature-Agent' header (Willison, 4 Aug 2025, secondary). No vendor policy read addresses how many agents one person may run.

findings.point: EU AI Act Art. 3(3)–(4): 'provider' develops or has developed and places on the market or puts into service 'under its own name or trademark'; 'deployer' uses a system 'under its authority except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity'.
findings.quote: using an AI system under its authority except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity
findings.implication_for_ratio: Most Moltbook owners are hobbyists; the personal-non-professional carve-out may take them out of 'deployer' entirely, leaving 88 agents with no AI Act addressee unless the owner counts as a provider (puts an agent into service under own name). Metric M10: share of owner_x_handle values that resolve to an organisation vs a person (via owner_x_bio where present; organisations only, per Vigilia's rules).

findings.point: EU AI Act Art. 50(1) and (5): providers must ensure systems interacting directly with natural persons inform them, unless obvious; information at first interaction.
findings.quote: Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system
findings.implication_for_ratio: Whether an agent-only feed that humans 'observe' is 'interacting directly with natural persons' is unsettled; the Commission's 20 July 2026 guidelines were not read in full. If it is, the ratio fixes where the duty lands: on whoever put each of the 88 into service, not on the one X handle that claimed them.

findings.point: EU AI Act Art. 99(4)(g): Art. 50 breaches carry the €15M/3% tier.
findings.quote: transparency obligations for providers and deployers pursuant to Article 50
findings.implication_for_ratio: Statutory maximum, not exposure. A fine needs an addressee; the ratio measures how many actors share each addressee.

findings.point: Swiss law: no AI act. Federal Council decided 12 Feb 2025 to ratify the Council of Europe AI Convention (signed 27 Mar 2025), sector-specific changes, consultation draft due end 2026; the Convention applies primarily to state actors.
findings.provision: admin.ch media release msg-id 104110 (12 Feb 2025); CETS 225 Art. 8 (transparency incl. identification of AI-generated content) and Art. 9 (accountability)
findings.quote: Switzerland intends to ratify the Council of Europe Convention on Artificial Intelligence (AI)
findings.implication_for_ratio: For a private Moltbook owner in Switzerland the Convention creates no direct duty today. The FDPIC (8 May 2025) states 'users have a legal right to know whether they are speaking or corresponding with a machine', grounded in the FADP (https://www.edoeb.admin.ch/en/update-current-legislation-directly-applicable-ai). Whether that reaches an owner of 88 agents on a US platform: needs legal review.

findings.point: Moltbook claiming flow (platform docs unreachable this session; Hashgraph Online and DataCamp as secondary): registration returns an API key plus claim URL and verification code; the human verifies email and posts the code on X; Moltbook then marks the agent claimed; before that the API answers 401 'Agent not yet claimed'.
findings.provision: is_claimed = the claim tweet was verified; owner_x_handle = the X account that posted it
findings.quote: Until the agent is claimed, Moltbook currently returns 401 with an 'Agent not yet claimed' error
findings.implication_for_ratio: The 'one X account, one agent' rule is asserted only by an unofficial fan site (moltsbooks.com) and must be verified against moltbook.com/skill.md or /terms. If it is real, every owner_x_handle with >1 agent in the archive is a rule breach measurable per row; if it is not, the ratio is policy-permitted.

findings.point: Wiz Research (disclosed 31 Jan–1 Feb 2026): owners table held 17,000+ rows against 1.5M agents; 35,000 emails; 1.5M API tokens; no check that an agent was AI.
findings.quote: The platform had no mechanism to verify whether an 'agent' was actually AI or just a human with a script.
findings.implication_for_ratio: 88:1 counts registered agents over owner rows, not claimed agents over verified handles. Wikipedia reports Moltbook's own counters at 6 Jun 2026: 206,839 human-verified of 2,895,874 registered (7.1% claimed). The archive can produce the honest denominator: posting agents per distinct handle, pre and post 2026-03-10 (Metric M7).

findings.point: Nearest empirical analogue for accounts-per-operator: Kumar et al., 'An Army of Me' (WWW 2017) — 3,656 sockpuppets in 1,623 groups on Disqus, about 2.25 accounts per puppetmaster. No published study of agent-to-owner ratios on an agent platform was found beyond Wiz's single figure.
findings.implication_for_ratio: 88:1 is roughly forty times the human sockpuppet baseline; that comparison is the headline the literature does not yet contain. Metric M11: name-entropy of agent names per handle (Kumar's sockpuppet heuristic) as a secondary automation signal.

lenses.who_is_provider_deployer: Four candidates, none settled. (1) The owner who writes the system prompt and runs OpenClaw: the most plausible 'provider' under Art. 3(3) — develops or has developed and puts into service under own name (the agent name and the X handle) — and simultaneously the 'deployer' under Art. 3(4), except that a hobbyist owner likely falls under the 'personal non-professional activity' carve-out from 'deployer' (text says) while the provider definition has no such carve-out (reasonable reading; needs legal review). (2) Moltbook/Meta: provider of the platform system (feed, ranking, reverse-CAPTCHA), not of each agent; the Art. 50(1) duty would attach to the platform only if the site itself is a system 'intended to interact directly with natural persons' (contested). (3) The model vendor (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, open models): general-purpose AI model provider with Art. 53 duties; not the Art. 50 addressee unless the model is the interacting system unchanged (reasonable reading). (4) OpenClaw: an open-source framework; Art. 2(12) exempts free and open-source AI systems 'unless ... placed on the market or put into service ... as an AI system that falls under Article 5 or 50' (recalled wording, not re-fetched this session; verify at EUR-Lex). Bottom line for the ratio: the only role with no exemption is the provider, and on Moltbook that role sits on an X handle; 17,000 handles for 1.5M agents means the addressee set is two orders of magnitude smaller than the actor set.

Medium on the Moltbook claim flow (platform docs unreachable; two secondary sources agree) and on the 6 Jun 2026 counters (Wikipedia only). synth.bottom_line: Both the EU AI Act and Swiss law create duties that a Moltbook agent's operator can breach, and neither creates any mechanism to find that operator. Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026, was left untouched by the Digital Omnibus, and carries a fine of up to EUR 15M or 3% (Art. 99(4)(g)) — but registration, naming and authorised-representative duties exist only for high-risk systems and GPAI models, and a hobbyist owner is carved out of "deployer" entirely (Art. 2(10)). Swiss law has no AI statute; its only hooks are FADP Art. 19 (a controller must name itself to data subjects) and UCA Art. 3(1)(s) (sellers online must publish identity). Wiz's 88:1 ratio (1.5M agents, ~17,000 owner rows) is therefore not a breach of anything; it is the measured size of the gap between the actors the law addresses and the persons it can reach. The Observatory Archive can turn that single figure into the first population-level measurement. This is a gap analysis, not a legal determination.

frame.question: Who is the provider of a Moltbook agent?
frame.answer: Four candidates, none settled by statute. Model vendor: provider of a GPAI model (Art. 3(63)), Chapter V duties, not the Art. 50 addressee for what an agent posts. OpenClaw framework: provider of an AI system placed on the market free of charge (Art. 3(3)); Art. 2(12) keeps open-source systems inside the Act where they fall under Art. 50, so the 50(1) design duty plausibly lands on the runtime. Owner writing the system prompt: on the words of Art. 3(3) ('has an AI system developed ... puts the AI system into service under its own name') a provider of that specific agent — the provider definition has no personal-use carve-out. Art. 25 (deployer becomes provider) is high-risk only and does not help. All three lenses agree the Commission FAQ and the July 2026 Guidelines do not reach the system-prompt case.
frame.provisions: Art. 3(3), 3(63), 3(66), 3(13); Art. 2(12) ('This Regulation does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences, unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as an AI system that falls under Article 5 or 50.'); Art. 25(1)
frame.status: reasonable reading; needs legal review at the owner/framework boundary

frame.question: Who is the deployer?
frame.answer: The owner, as the person 'using an AI system under its authority' — except that Art. 3(4) and Art. 2(10) remove natural persons acting in a 'purely personal non-professional activity', and the Commission FAQ says a person posting AI content on social media in a personal capacity is outside the Act. A hobbyist running 88 agents has no 50(4) duty. Professional owners (companies, marketers, researchers) keep it, and they are indistinguishable from hobbyists in the archive. The platform (Moltbook, Meta since 2026-03-10) is neither provider nor deployer of the agents; it is a DSA hosting question (recital 136) and holds the only owner table, with no AI Act duty to keep or disclose it.
frame.provisions: Art. 3(4); Art. 2(10) ('This Regulation does not apply to obligations of deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity.'); recital 136
frame.status: text says (carve-out); reasonable reading (platform outside the Regulation)

frame.question: Does Article 50 apply agent-to-agent?
frame.answer: Not on the Commission's own reading: the FAQ places systems operating 'through machine-to-machine communication, or without direct contact with people' outside 50(1). Where humans observe the public feed, three positions: (i) the platform's 'every account is an agent' framing satisfies the 'obvious' exception on-platform — but the Commission says that exception is read restrictively, and Wiz showed humans could post as agents; (ii) the exception fails once a post is quoted elsewhere; (iii) 50(4) (published text informing the public on matters of public interest) is triggered by topic, not audience, and its editorial-responsibility exemption cannot be claimed when no natural or legal person is on record for any post (recital 134). The EU lens labels the observer case contested per surface; the literature lens labels the whole question contested. They do not disagree on substance.
frame.provisions: Art. 50(1) first sentence; Art. 50(4) second subparagraph; Art. 50(5); recitals 132, 134
frame.status: text says (machine-to-machine outside 50(1), per FAQ); contested (human observers; 50(4) on an agent-majority audience)

frame.question: What does 17,000 owners behind 1.5M agents mean for enforceability?
frame.answer: A fine needs an addressee. The 'if the offender is an undertaking' clause in Art. 99 shows natural persons are fineable, but a market surveillance authority must first identify the person behind a handle, and the Act gives it no tool for a non-high-risk system: no registry (Art. 49/71), no name-on-product (Art. 16(b)), no authorised representative (Art. 22) apply. Of the ~17,000, only EU-established owners are caught with certainty (Art. 2(1)(b)); third-country owners depend on the contested 'output used in the Union' limb (Art. 2(1)(c)). The complaint right (Art. 85) is real but has no addressee unless the platform discloses identity — a DSA/GDPR question. The ratio also overstates accountability coverage: Wiz counts registered agents over owner rows; Moltbook's own counters (6 Jun 2026, via Wikipedia) showed 7.1% of registered agents human-verified. Against the only empirical analogue, Kumar et al.'s 2.25 accounts per human sockpuppeteer, 88:1 is roughly forty times the human baseline.
frame.provisions: Art. 99(4)(g) ('up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3 % of its total worldwide annual turnover ... whichever is higher'); Art. 99(1), (6); Art. 2(1)(a)-(c), (g); Art. 49(1), 16(b), 22(1), 85(1)
frame.status: text says (penalty tier, registry limits); contested (territorial reach via reading in the EU); reasonable reading (enforceable population = platform user table)

frame.question: What does Swiss law add?
frame.answer: No AI statute; the Federal Council (12 Feb 2025) chose ratification of CETS 225 plus sectoral amendments, with an EJPD consultation draft due end-2026 whose named pillars include 'Transparenz' — the place to argue for owner traceability. CETS 225 (signed 27 Mar 2025, not ratified) binds the state and asks only for notification of AI interaction (Art. 15(2)) and identification of AI content (Art. 8), never of the person behind an agent. Today's hooks: FADP Art. 19(2)(a) — a controller collecting personal data must give 'the controller's identity and contact details', fine up to CHF 250,000 on complaint (Art. 60(1)); UCA Art. 3(1)(s) — anyone offering goods or services online must publish identity and email; OR 41 fault liability attributes an agent's harm to its operator, with the ratio itself evidence on whether one human can meet the standard of care over 88 personas. All presuppose an identified defendant. Both lenses agree: an 88:1 ratio is legally invisible in Switzerland in September 2026.
frame.status: text says (statutes, Convention); reasonable reading (no draft published by 23 Sep 2026 — admin.ch unreachable, verify); contested (OR 55/101 by analogy to software agents; whether a post is an 'automated individual decision')

frame.question: What does the literature propose?
frame.answer: Chan et al. (2024, 2025) name the missing piece: visibility into 'by whom' an agent is used, via agent identifiers carrying responsible-party metadata, activity logs and identity binding. South et al. (2025) propose OAuth-style delegation credentials so each agent action carries a verifiable chain to a human principal; Moltbook's only credential is the API key and the human link is an out-of-band tweet, deletable after verification. A2A v1.0 AgentCards carry a provider organisation and card signatures but defer verifying the organisation to deployment policy. Otsuka et al. (2026) list 'recursive delegation accountability' as an open gap with no empirical number attached. Vendor policies (Anthropic, Google) place the disclosure duty on the operator and say nothing about how many agents one person may run. No published study measures agent-to-owner ratios on an agent platform; the archive-derived metrics below would be new.

synth.what_the_ratio_implies: The ratio is a measurement of the gap between actors and addressees, not evidence of any breach. On the EU side the actor set (agents) is two orders of magnitude larger than the largest possible addressee set (owner handles), and that set shrinks further to the intersection of EU-established and professionally acting owners, which the archive cannot see directly. The only role with no personal-use exemption is 'provider', and whether a system-prompt author holds it is the unresolved question that decides whether 88 agents have any EU addressee at all. On the Swiss side the ratio matters only after a defendant is known, as evidence on the fault element (Sorgfalt) under OR 41. For the brief: 88:1 should be presented as Wiz's registration-era figure, then replaced with the archive's honest denominators (posting agents per distinct claimed handle, pre and post 2026-03-10), and set against Kumar et al.'s 2.25 human sockpuppet baseline. Where lenses diverge: the literature lens leans towards owner-as-provider as 'most plausible'; the EU lens holds it at 'contested, needs legal review'. The brief should carry the EU lens's caution.
