synth.markdown:
## The legal frame: an attribution gap, not a breach

**Bottom line.** Both the EU AI Act and Swiss law impose duties that the operator of a Moltbook agent can breach, and neither gives anyone a way to find that operator. Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026, survived the Digital Omnibus untouched, and carries a maximum fine of EUR 15 million or 3% of turnover (Art. 99(4)(g)). But every registration, naming and authorised-representative duty in the Act is confined to high-risk systems and general-purpose models, and a natural person running agents as a hobby is carved out of "deployer" altogether (Art. 2(10)). Swiss law has no AI statute; its only hooks are the FADP (a controller must name itself to data subjects) and the Unfair Competition Act (a seller online must publish identity). Wiz's 88:1 figure — roughly 1.5 million agents against about 17,000 owner rows — is therefore not evidence of any violation. It is the measured distance between the actors the law addresses and the persons it can reach. *This is a gap analysis by a disclosed AI agent, not a legal determination; every item marked "needs legal review" goes to counsel before publication.*

### Six questions

**1. Who is the provider?** — *reasonable reading; needs legal review.* The Act defines a provider as one who "develops an AI system ... or that has an AI system ... developed and places it on the market or puts the AI system into service under its own name or trademark, whether for payment or free of charge" (Art. 3(3)). Four candidates. The model vendor is a GPAI-model provider (Art. 3(63)) with Chapter V duties, not the addressee for what an agent posts. The OpenClaw framework is a provider of a system placed on the market free of charge; Art. 2(12) states the Regulation "does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences, unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as an AI system that falls under Article 5 or 50", so the 50(1) design duty plausibly lands on the runtime. The owner who writes the system prompt and runs the agent under a handle fits the words "has an AI system developed ... puts [it] into service under its own name" — and the provider definition has no personal-use carve-out. Art. 25, which turns deployers into providers, is high-risk only and does not resolve this. All three lenses agree the Commission FAQ and the July 2026 Guidelines do not address the system-prompt case. The literature lens calls owner-as-provider "most plausible"; the EU lens holds it at contested. The brief should carry the caution.

**2. Who is the deployer?** — *text says (carve-out); reasonable reading (platform).* The owner, "using an AI system under its authority" (Art. 3(4)) — unless a natural person "using AI systems in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity" (Art. 2(10)), whom the Commission FAQ puts outside the Act entirely. A hobbyist with 88 agents owes nothing under 50(4); a company, marketer or researcher does, and the two are indistinguishable in the archive. Moltbook (Meta since 2026-03-10) is neither provider nor deployer of the agents. It is a DSA hosting question (recital 136), holds the only owner table, and has no AI Act duty to keep or disclose it.

**3. Does Article 50 apply agent-to-agent?** — *text says (FAQ); contested (observers).* The Commission FAQ places systems operating "through machine-to-machine communication, or without direct contact with people" outside 50(1). For the human who reads the feed: the platform's "every account is an agent" framing may satisfy the "obvious" exception on-platform, but the Commission reads that exception restrictively and Wiz showed humans could post as agents via a plain POST request — recital 132's impersonation risk, inverted. Off-platform, once a post is quoted, the exception fails. 50(4) (text "published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest") turns on topic, not audience; its editorial-responsibility exemption cannot be claimed when no natural or legal person is on record for any post (recital 134).

**4. What does 17,000 behind 1.5 million mean for enforceability?** — *text says (tiers, registry limits); contested (territorial reach).* A fine needs an addressee. Natural persons are fineable — the clause "if the offender is an undertaking" implies a fixed cap for those who are not — but an authority must first identify the person behind a handle, and for a non-high-risk system the Act offers no registry (Art. 49/71), no name-on-product (Art. 16(b)), no authorised representative (Art. 22). Only EU-established owners are caught with certainty (Art. 2(1)(b)); third-country owners depend on whether a post read in the EU is output "used in the Union" (Art. 2(1)(c)), on which no guidance exists. The Art. 85 complaint right has no addressee unless the platform discloses identity — a DSA/GDPR path, outside this Regulation. The ratio also overstates coverage: Wiz counts registered agents over owner rows, while Moltbook's own counters on 6 June 2026 (via Wikipedia, primary not read) showed 7.1% of registered agents human-verified. Against the one empirical analogue — Kumar et al. (2017), 2.25 accounts per human sockpuppeteer on Disqus — 88:1 is roughly forty times the human baseline.

**5. What does Swiss law add?** — *text says (statutes); reasonable reading (no draft yet); contested (liability analogies).* No AI act. On 12 February 2025 the Federal Council chose to ratify CETS 225 (signed 27 March 2025, not ratified), amend sectoral law, and table a consultation draft by end-2026 whose named pillars include "Transparenz" — the venue for an owner-traceability argument. The Convention asks Parties to "seek to ensure ... persons interacting with artificial intelligence systems are notified that they are interacting with such systems" (Art. 15(2)) and to address "identification of content generated by artificial intelligence systems" (Art. 8); neither concerns the person behind the agent. Today's hooks: FADP Art. 19(2) — a controller must give "the controller's identity and contact details", fine up to CHF 250,000 on complaint (Art. 60(1)); UCA Art. 3(1)(s) — a person offering goods or services online must give "clear and complete details of their identity and their contact address including their email address"; OR 41(1) — "Any person who unlawfully causes damage to another, whether wilfully or negligently, is obliged to provide compensation", with the ratio itself evidence on whether one human can meet the standard of care over 88 personas. Every one of these presupposes an identified defendant. Both Swiss-facing lenses agree: an 88:1 ratio is legally invisible in Switzerland in September 2026.

**6. What does the literature propose?** — *text says.* Chan et al. (2024) name the missing piece as visibility into "by whom" agents are used, through identifiers with responsible-party metadata, activity logs and identity binding (2025). South et al. (2025) propose OAuth-style delegation credentials so each action carries a verifiable chain to a human principal; Moltbook's only credential is the API key, and the human link is an out-of-band tweet, deletable after verification. A2A v1.0 AgentCards carry a provider organisation and signatures but defer verifying the organisation to deployment policy. Otsuka et al. (2026) list delegation accountability as an open gap with no number attached. Vendor policies (Anthropic, Google) put the disclosure duty on the operator and say nothing about fleet size. No published study measures agent-to-owner ratios on an agent platform.

### What Study C should compute

From `agents` (`is_claimed`, `owner_x_handle`, `created_at`, `description`, `name`) and `posts` (author key, `created_at`, karma), split at the 2026-03-10 partition: **M1** accountability-resolvable share of posting agents and of posts (claimed, handle non-null); **M2** posting agents per distinct handle — the honest replacement for 88:1; **M3** concentration (Gini, top-1%/10% share, maximum agents on one handle); **M4** posts by unclaimed agents — if non-zero the 401 gate was a claim, not a fact; **M5** registration bursts per handle within one minute, Wiz's loop signature; **M6** share of descriptions naming a model, framework or operator — the A2A provider field measured after the fact; **M7** organisation versus person among claimed handles, organisations only; **M8** karma concentration by handle (OWASP ASI10 precondition); **M9** name-entropy per handle against the 2.25:1 sockpuppet baseline. Distributions only. **No handle-level table is ever published**: owner handles are personal data under FADP Art. 5(a) and the Logistep test, and Vigilia's own rule is organisations and public roles only.

### Legal review before publication

Owner as provider under Art. 3(3) (decides whether 88:1 has any EU addressee). "Output used in the Union" for posts read in the EU. The "obvious" exception for human observers. The Guidelines' reported "on whose behalf" rule — known only from law-firm notes; read the PDF. Art. 2(12) and amended Art. 113 re-read on EUR-Lex (both read on mirrors). Moltbook/Meta's DSA status and any duty to disclose owner identity. National penalty regimes for natural persons. Swiss: whether the EJPD draft appeared between 22 July and 23 September 2026 (admin.ch was unreachable); CETS 225 entry-into-force and Swiss non-ratification (coe.int not fetched); FADP territorial scope; OR 55/101 analogy (no case law; the unisg paper unread). Vigilia's own processing of handles (FADP Art. 19/20/27) and ZGB 61(2) no. 3 registration once foreign funds exceed CHF 100,000 over two years. Moltbook's "one account, one agent" rule — asserted only by a fan site; read skill.md and /terms. The 17,000 versus 35,000-email discrepancy in Wiz. Which FDPIC statement carries the "right to know you are talking to a machine" line (three dates cited across lenses). Fedlex English texts are unofficial; cite German, French or Italian for anything binding.

### Confidence

High on the statutory quotations (Art. 2, 3, 50, 99; FADP, UCA, OR; CETS 225 from the EU Official Journal) and on the Omnibus leaving Article 50 and 2 August 2026 untouched. Medium on role allocation and on the Swiss "no draft yet". Low on the Guidelines' agent paragraph, the platform's claim rules, and the 6 June 2026 counters. The 88:1 figure is Wiz's, from an early-2026 snapshot, about registration rather than activity; the archive metrics would be the first population-level measurement.

verdicts.claim: Article 50(1) obliges providers to ensure systems intended to interact directly with natural persons inform them they are interacting with an AI system, unless obvious; it applies from 2 August 2026.
verdicts.evidence_quote: Article 50(1): "Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use. This obligation shall not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties, unless those systems are available for the public to report a criminal offence." — Article 113: "It shall apply from 2 August 2026. However: (a) Chapters I and II shall apply from 2 February 2025; (b) Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, Chapter VII and Chapter XII and Article 78 shall apply from 2 August 2025, with the exception of Article 101; (c) Article 6(1) and the corresponding obligations in this Regulation shall apply from 2 August 2027."
verdicts.note: Text says. Re-fetched from the primary source: the EUR-Lex ELI page for Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (OJ L, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024), read in a browser session because the fetch tool truncated the page before Article 49; the quotes above are copied from the live page text. Both halves of the claim hold. (1) The duty: Article 50(1), first sentence, matches the claim in substance. Two precisions the claim compresses: the "unless obvious" test is the objective standard of "a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use", and the second sentence carves out AI systems authorised by law for criminal-offence detection/investigation/prosecution (unless open to the public for reporting offences). (2) The date: Article 50 sits in Chapter IV ("CHAPTER IV TRANSPARENCY OBLIGATIONS FOR PROVIDERS AND DEPLOYERS OF CERTAIN AI SYSTEMS" immediately precedes "Article 50"). Article 113's general rule is "It shall apply from 2 August 2026", and Chapter IV is in none of the three exceptions (a) Chapters I and II, (b) Chapter III Section 4, Chapters V, VII, XII and Article 78, (c) Article 6(1). So 2 August 2026 for Article 50 is the text as published in the OJ, by direct reading of Articles 50 and 113 together. Caveat for the synthesis step: this verifies the OJ text as adopted on 13 June 2024. Whether any later amending act (the "Digital Omnibus" referred to in Vigilia's deadlines.ts) has since altered the Article 50 application date is not established by this fetch; the workspace's standing position is that it did not touch Article 50, and that should be confirmed against the consolidated EUR-Lex version or the amending act's own text before it is printed as current law. Confidence in the claim as stated against the OJ text: high. Vigilia is not a law firm; this is a gap-analysis reading, not a legal determination.

verdicts.claim: The Commission's Article 50 FAQ places systems operating through machine-to-machine communication, or without direct contact with people, outside the 50(1) obligation.
verdicts.evidence_quote: AI systems operating solely in the background, through machine-to-machine communication, or without direct contact with people, fall outside the scope of this obligation.
verdicts.note: Text says. Re-fetched 2026-09-23 from the primary page (title "Transparency obligations under Article 50 of the AI Act", page shows last update 24 July 2026). The sentence appears in the answer to the FAQ question "When do providers of AI systems have to inform people they are interacting with an AI system?", which is the 50(1) duty; the same answer notes the duty runs from the start of the interaction unless it is "obvious". Two independent fetches returned the identical sentence. Caveats for the synthesis step: (1) this is Commission guidance, not the statutory text of Article 50(1) (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, EUR-Lex CELEX 32024R1689) and is not legally binding; whether an agent-to-agent platform such as Moltbook, where agents' output is later read by humans on a public website, counts as "without direct contact with people" is a reasonable-reading question the FAQ sentence does not settle — needs legal review before Vigilia states it as a finding. (2) The FAQ wording is "solely in the background ... or without direct contact with people"; the claim's paraphrase drops "solely" and "in the background", which narrows the exclusion slightly in the original. (3) Article 50(2) (marking of synthetic content) and 50(4) (deepfakes / public-interest text) are separate duties not addressed by this sentence.

verdicts.claim: Article 2(10) excludes obligations of deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in a purely personal non-professional activity; the provider definition in Art. 3(3) has no equivalent carve-out.
verdicts.evidence_quote: Art. 2(10): "This Regulation does not apply to obligations of deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity." | Art. 3(3): "'provider' means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body that develops an AI system or a general-purpose AI model or that has an AI system or a general-purpose AI model developed and places it on the market or puts the AI system into service under its own name or trademark, whether for payment or free of charge;" | Art. 3(4): "'deployer' means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body using an AI system under its authority except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity;" | Art. 3(11): "'putting into service' means the supply of an AI system for first use directly to the deployer or for own use in the Union for its intended purpose;"
verdicts.note: TEXT SAYS: both halves of the claim hold on the primary text, re-fetched 2026-09-23 from EUR-Lex (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, CELEX:32024R1689). The ELI URL given (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng) resolves to the same Official Journal document but the fetch tool truncated it at recital (67), so the quotations were taken from EUR-Lex's own HTML rendering of the identical CELEX document via curl and grep; no secondary source was used. (1) Art. 2(10) is verbatim as claimed, except the statute says "in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity" (the claim drops "in the course of a"). (2) Art. 3(3) 'provider' contains no personal/non-professional exception; it is drafted as "natural or legal person" and expressly covers supply "whether for payment or free of charge". By contrast the deployer definition in Art. 3(4) carries the carve-out a second time ("except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity"), so the asymmetry appears in both the scope article and the definitions article. REASONABLE READING (for the Moltbook attribution-gap study): a natural person who runs an off-the-shelf agent for personal amusement is outside the Act as a deployer, but a natural person who builds or has built an agent and "puts it into service" under their own name — Art. 3(11) includes supply "for own use in the Union for its intended purpose" — is not excluded by the Act's text from provider status on personal-use grounds. Whether a hobbyist's self-built Moltbook agent is "developed" and "put into service under its own name or trademark" is a fact question and CONTESTED; the Act's other provider-side exclusions in Art. 2 (research/testing before placing on the market, Art. 2(8); free and open-source systems, Art. 2(12), which by its own terms does not lift Art. 50 obligations) are not keyed to natural-person personal use, but I could not extract those two paragraphs verbatim in this run, so treat that last sentence as from memory, NEEDS LEGAL REVIEW before it is published. Art. 50 itself was not re-fetched here; the Article 50(2)/(4) provider-versus-deployer split for synthetic content and its interaction with Art. 2(10) is the load-bearing question for the policy brief and should be quoted verbatim in the synthesis step, not paraphrased from this note. Confidence that the claim as stated is textually accurate: high.

verdicts.claim: Article 2(12) exempts free and open-source AI systems unless placed on the market or put into service as high-risk or as a system falling under Article 5 or 50 — so an open-source agent runtime stays inside Article 50.
verdicts.evidence_quote: Article 2(12): "This Regulation does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences, unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as an AI system that falls under Article 5 or 50."
verdicts.note: Text says (first half of the claim): re-fetched 2026-09-23 from the stated source; the page reproduces Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Article 2 with thirteen paragraphs and paragraph 12 reads exactly as quoted. The open-source carve-out is conditional: it falls away where the system is placed on the market or put into service as high-risk, or as a system under Article 5 (prohibited practices) or Article 50 (transparency). Reasonable reading (second half of the claim): an open-source agent runtime is not exempted from Article 50 by the licence alone; whether Article 50 duties actually attach depends on the runtime meeting Article 50's own triggers (e.g. Art. 50(1) systems intended to interact directly with natural persons, Art. 50(2) synthetic-content generation, Art. 50(4) deployer duties) and on the "placed on the market / put into service" conditions of Art. 3(9)-(11) — the claim's phrase "stays inside Article 50" is an inference, not statutory text. Caveat on source hierarchy: artificialintelligenceact.eu is a Future of Life Institute reproduction, not the Official Journal. A same-session fetch of EUR-Lex (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng) returned only the recitals before truncation, so the verbatim wording was not re-confirmed against EUR-Lex here; the reproduction matches the OJ wording as known, and the ELI link is the citation to carry into the paper. Needs legal review: whether a specific Moltbook-hosted open-source runtime is a "provider" placing a system on the market (Art. 3(3), 3(9)) versus a mere code publication — that determination is outside Vigilia's gap-analysis frame. Confidence: high on the text, medium on the inference.

verdicts.claim: Breaches of Article 50 carry administrative fines of up to EUR 15,000,000 or, for undertakings, 3% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)(g)); statutory maximum, not exposure.
verdicts.evidence_quote: Art. 99(4): "Non-compliance with any of the following provisions related to operators or notified bodies, other than those laid down in Articles 5, shall be subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher: [...] (g) transparency obligations for providers and deployers pursuant to Article 50." Art. 99(6): "In the case of SMEs, including start-ups, each fine referred to in this Article shall be up to the percentages or amount referred to in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5, whichever thereof is lower."
verdicts.note: Text says. Source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Official Journal PDF from EUR-Lex (OJ L, 12.7.2024, page 115/144, ELI http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), Chapter XII, Article 99 "Penalties", paragraph 4, point (g). The claim's figures (EUR 15 000 000 / 3 % / "whichever is higher") and the mapping to Art. 99(4)(g) match the primary text verbatim. Two qualifications in the same article support the "statutory maximum, not exposure" framing: Art. 99(1) leaves the rules on penalties to Member States ("effective, proportionate and dissuasive", with regard to SMEs), Art. 99(6) inverts the rule for SMEs and start-ups to whichever is LOWER, and Art. 99(7) lists the circumstances (nature, gravity, duration, size, cooperation, intent or negligence) that set the amount in each case. Neighbouring tiers also confirmed on pp. 115-116: Art. 99(3) EUR 35 000 000 / 7 % (Article 5 prohibited practices); Art. 99(5) EUR 7 500 000 / 1 % (incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities). Art. 101(1) separately gives the Commission a 3 % / EUR 15 000 000 ceiling for providers of general-purpose AI models. Method note: the EUR-Lex HTML endpoints (eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng and legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML) were fetched but truncated before Article 99; verification was done by reading pages 115-117 of the OJ PDF downloaded from eur-lex.europa.eu in this session, not from memory or a secondary source. No legal review needed for the figures themselves; how a fine would be set in a given case is for a lawyer and outside a gap analysis.

verdicts.claim: Registration in the EU database (Art. 49/71), name-and-address marking (Art. 16(b)) and authorised representatives (Art. 22) apply only to high-risk AI systems; no traceability duty exists for a non-high-risk social-media agent.
verdicts.evidence_quote: Art. 16: "Providers of high-risk AI systems shall: [...] (b) indicate on the high-risk AI system or, where that is not possible, on its packaging or its accompanying documentation, as applicable, their name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, the address at which they can be contacted;" — Art. 22(1): "Prior to making their high-risk AI systems available on the Union market, providers established in third countries shall, by written mandate, appoint an authorised representative which is established in the Union." — Art. 49(1): "Before placing on the market or putting into service a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, with the exception of high-risk AI systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III, the provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative shall register themselves and their system in the EU database referred to in Article 71." — Art. 49(2): "Before placing on the market or putting into service an AI system for which the provider has concluded that it is not high-risk according to Article 6(3), that provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative shall register themselves and that system in the EU database referred to in Article 71." — Art. 50(2): "Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content, shall ensure that the outputs of the AI system are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated."
verdicts.note:
SOURCE AND METHOD. The ELI landing page (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng) loaded but the fetch tool truncated it inside the recitals, before any article. I therefore downloaded the full consolidated HTML of the same act from EUR-Lex (CELEX:32024R1689, the URL above, 1.26 MB) and extracted the articles from the local copy. All quotations are verbatim from that primary text. No secondary source was used.

VERDICT: the claim is half right and half wrong, so it fails as written.

PART 1 — "Art. 49/71, 16(b) and 22 apply only to high-risk AI systems".
- Art. 16(b) — TEXT SAYS: the article opens "Providers of high-risk AI systems shall" and (b) is the name/trade-name/address marking. Only high-risk. Confirmed.
- Art. 22(1) — TEXT SAYS: the authorised-representative duty is on "providers [of high-risk AI systems] established in third countries". Only high-risk. Confirmed. Caveat: Art. 54(1) creates a parallel duty for third-country providers of general-purpose AI MODELS ("Prior to placing a general-purpose AI model on the Union market, providers established in third countries shall, by written mandate, appoint an authorised representative which is established in the Union"). That binds the model provider (e.g. a frontier lab), not the operator of a social-media agent built on the model, but a claim that authorised representatives are a high-risk-only device is incomplete.
- Art. 49/71 — TEXT SAYS the claim is INACCURATE: registration is not limited to high-risk systems. Art. 49(2) requires registration of an Annex III system "for which the provider has concluded that it is not high-risk according to Article 6(3)", and Art. 71(1) says the database also contains "AI systems that are not considered as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(3) and which are registered in accordance with Article 6(4) and Article 49". Art. 49(1) is also narrower than "all high-risk": it covers Annex III systems only ("a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, with the exception of high-risk AI systems referred to in point 2 of Annex III"); Annex I product-safety systems are outside Art. 49(1). REASONABLE READING: a social-media posting agent is not an Annex III use case, so neither 49(1) nor 49(2) reaches it in practice — but the statement "only high-risk" is wrong as a description of the text and should be rewritten as "only Annex III systems, whether classified high-risk or de-classified under Art. 6(3)".

PART 2 — "no traceability duty exists for a non-high-risk social-media agent".
- TEXT SAYS this is wrong as stated, for the meaning of "traceability" that matters to a register of disclosure: Art. 50 is risk-class-independent. Art. 50(1): "Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed in such a way that the natural persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect". Art. 50(2) (quoted above) requires machine-readable marking of synthetic text "detectable as artificially generated or manipulated", subject to the carve-out for assistive editing that does "not substantially alter the input data provided by the deployer or the semantics thereof". Art. 50(4), second subparagraph: "Deployers of an AI system that generates or manipulates text which is published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest shall disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated", unless the content "has undergone a process of human review or editorial control and where a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility". These are provenance/detectability duties on the OUTPUT.
- REASONABLE READING: what the text does NOT impose on a non-high-risk agent is any duty to identify the provider, deployer or owner by name and contactable address (that is Art. 16(b), high-risk only), nor to appear in a public database (Art. 49/71, Annex III only). So the accurate formulation is: "for a non-high-risk, non-Annex III social-media agent the AI Act imposes content-provenance duties (Art. 50(1), (2), (4)) but no operator-identification or registration duty; the attribution gap is a gap in who-is-behind-it, not in whether-it-is-AI." That formulation is what the Moltbook attribution-gap study should carry.
- CONTESTED / NEEDS LEGAL REVIEW: (a) whether an autonomous agent posting on a platform like Moltbook is an "AI system intended to interact directly with natural persons" under 50(1) when its readers are mostly other agents — the text turns on intent and on the "obvious" exception; (b) whether Art. 50(2) applies to a US-established agent operator at all (territorial scope is Art. 2(1), not re-fetched here); (c) whether Art. 50(4) "matters of public interest" reaches social posts; (d) whether the Digital Omnibus changed any of this — CLAUDE.md's standing position is that Art. 50 still applies from 2 August 2026 and the deferral touched high-risk only; that was not re-verified in this pass and should be checked against the Omnibus text before publication. Swiss law was not examined here.

CONFIDENCE: high on Part 1 (verbatim text, three articles quoted); high that Part 2 is wrong as worded (Art. 50 quoted verbatim); medium on the reasonable reading of "traceability", which depends on a definition the claim did not supply. This is a gap analysis, not a legal determination.

verdicts.claim: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI) deferred Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028 but left Article 50(1), (3), (4), (5) and the 2 August 2026 application date unchanged.
verdicts.evidence_quote: Article 1, point (40): "in Article 113, the third paragraph is amended as follows: (a) point (a) is replaced by the following: '(a) Chapters I and II shall apply from 2 February 2025, with the exception of Article 5(1), first subparagraph, points (ba) and (bb), and Article 5(1a) and (1b) which shall apply from 2 December 2026;'; (b) point (c) is replaced by the following: '(c) Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3, with the exception of Article 6(5), shall apply from: (i) 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III; and (ii) 2 August 2028 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(1) and Annex I;'; (c) the following point is added: '(d) Articles 102 to 110 shall apply from 27 July 2026.'" — Article 1, point (20): "in Article 50, paragraph 7 is replaced by the following: [...]" (the only point of Article 1 that touches Article 50). Recital (40): "Article 113 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 establishes the dates of entry into force and application of that Regulation, in particular that the general date of application is 2 August 2026."
verdicts.note: TEXT SAYS. Verified against the OJ PDF of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (OJ L, 24.7.2026, 41 pp., ELI http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2026/1744/oj), fetched from the EUR-Lex ELI URL and read page by page (pp. 1-3, 12-41; the operative Article 1 spans pp. 15-36 and was read in full). Method note: WebFetch's summarizer truncated the HTML and returned inconsistent point numbers (1(13)/1(53) for Article 113; 1(41) for Article 50) — those were hallucinated; the PDF is authoritative and the correct points are 1(20) and 1(40). Findings: (1) Deferral: Article 1(40)(b) replaces Article 113, third paragraph, point (c) — "Chapter III, Sections 1, 2, and 3, with the exception of Article 6(5)" applies from 2 December 2027 (Article 6(2)/Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (Article 6(1)/Annex I). Reasonable reading: Chapter III Sections 1-3 are the classification rules, requirements and provider/deployer obligations for high-risk systems, i.e. "high-risk obligations" as the claim puts it; the text does not use the word "obligations". (2) Article 50(1), (3), (4), (5) unchanged: the only amendment to Article 50 in the whole act is Article 1(20), which replaces paragraph 7 (codes of practice; the Commission "may adopt an implementing act specifying common rules" only if it deems a code inadequate). No point of Article 1 touches paragraphs 1-6. (3) 2 August 2026 unchanged: the amending act touches only the THIRD paragraph of Article 113 (points (a), (c), new (d)); the second paragraph of Article 113 ("It shall apply from 2 August 2026") is not amended, and recital (40) restates "the general date of application is 2 August 2026". Article 50 sits in Chapter IV, which is governed by that general date. (4) One adjacent fact the claim correctly omits but a synthesis should carry: Article 1(39)(b) inserts Article 111(4): "Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content, that have been placed on the market before 2 August 2026 shall take the necessary steps in order to comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026." That is a four-month transitional for Article 50(2) marking only, for systems already on the market; it does not reach 50(1), (3), (4) or (5). (5) Entry into force: Article 4 — third day after publication in the OJ (published 24.7.2026, so 27 July 2026, consistent with new Article 113(3)(d) "Articles 102 to 110 shall apply from 27 July 2026"). Confidence: high on all three limbs of the claim; the text is direct. For deadlines.ts: the "Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026" line stands; add the 2 December 2026 Article 50(2) transitional for pre-existing generative systems if not already there, and note Annex I deferral is 2 August 2028 (not 2027). Nothing here needs legal review beyond the standing caveat that "high-risk obligations" is a gloss on "Chapter III, Sections 1, 2 and 3".

verdicts.claim: Wiz Research found the Moltbook owners table held about 17,000 rows against roughly 1.5 million registered agents (88:1), 1.5 million exposed API keys, and no mechanism to verify that an agent was AI.
verdicts.evidence_quote: "The owners table contained personal information for 17,000+ users" ... "Moltbook reported 1.5 million registered agents" ... "the database revealed only 17,000 human owners behind them - an 88:1 ratio" ... "1.5 million API authentication tokens" ... "The platform had no mechanism to verify whether an 'agent' was actually AI or just a human with a script."
verdicts.note: Text says. Primary source re-fetched 2026-09-23: Wiz blog post "Hacking Moltbook: The AI Social Network Any Human Can Control", by Gal Nagli, dated 2 February 2026. All five elements of the claim appear verbatim or near-verbatim. Two precision points for the synthesis: (1) the 1.5 million agent count is Moltbook's own reported figure as relayed by Wiz, not an independent Wiz count; the 88:1 ratio is Wiz's computation from that figure against the 17,000+ owner rows. (2) Wiz writes "1.5 million API authentication tokens"; the claim's "API keys" is a fair paraphrase but cite the article's wording. The article also states "humans could post content disguised as 'AI agents' via a basic POST request" and "Anyone could register millions of agents with a simple loop and no rate limiting" — useful for the attribution-gap study (Study C). Confidence: high.

verdicts.claim: The Swiss Federal Council decided on 12 February 2025 to ratify the Council of Europe AI Convention, pursue sector-specific amendments, and prepare a consultation draft by end-2026 covering transparency, data protection, non-discrimination and supervision.
verdicts.evidence_quote: "Published on 12 February 2025 — AI regulation: Federal Council to ratify Council of Europe Convention. Bern, 12.2.2025 - Switzerland intends to ratify the Council of Europe Convention on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and to make the necessary amendments to Swiss law. [...] The Federal Council spoke out in favour of this approach at its meeting on 12 February. [...] Where legislative changes are needed, they should be as sector-specific as possible. Only key areas relevant to fundamental rights, such as data protection, will be subject to general, cross-sectoral regulation. [...] The Federal Council has decided on the following next steps. The FDJP will draft a bill for consultation with DETEC and the FDFA by the end of 2026. The bill will implement the Council of Europe's AI Convention by defining the necessary legal measures, in particular in the areas of transparency, data protection, non-discrimination and supervision. DETEC, together with the FDJP, the FDFA and the EAER, will also draw up a plan by the end of 2026 for further measures non-legally-binding measures."
verdicts.note: Text says. Primary source re-fetched 2026-09-23 and rendered in a browser; every element of the claim appears verbatim: the 12 February 2025 date and meeting, the intent to ratify the CoE AI Convention, "as sector-specific as possible" for legislative changes, a bill "for consultation ... by the end of 2026", and the four named areas (transparency, data protection, non-discrimination, supervision). Two precision points for the synthesis: (1) the release says "intends to ratify" / "spoke out in favour of this approach" — a Federal Council policy decision on parameters and next steps, not the act of ratification itself, which needs a bill and Parliament; (2) the drafting mandate is to the FDJP with DETEC and the FDFA, and a separate DETEC-led plan for non-binding measures is also due end-2026. Access notes: the given /gov/en/...msg-id-104110 URL now redirects to https://www.admin.ch/en/nsb?id=104110 (same release, same publisher); curl returns an Akamai 403 and WebFetch returns only the lead paragraph, so a full browser render was required to read the body. Whether the end-2026 consultation is still on schedule as of September 2026 is not stated by this page and was not checked — reasonable reading only, and a follow-up on admin.ch/fedlex would settle it.

verdicts.claim: CETS 225 Art. 15(2) asks Parties to ensure persons are notified they are interacting with an AI system, and Art. 8 covers identification of AI-generated content; neither requires identifying the person behind an agent.
verdicts.evidence_quote: Article 15(2): "Each Party shall seek to ensure that, as appropriate for the context, persons interacting with artificial intelligence systems are notified that they are interacting with such systems rather than with a human." Article 8: "Each Party shall adopt or maintain measures to ensure that adequate transparency and oversight requirements tailored to the specific contexts and risks are in place in respect of activities within the lifecycle of artificial intelligence systems, including with regard to the identification of content generated by artificial intelligence systems."
verdicts.note: Re-fetched the primary source twice (the ELI URL and the OJ HTML at https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=OJ:L_202601081); both return identical text. Document: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law, OJ L 2026/1081, 13.5.2026, document 22026A01081 (the EU's publication of the CETS 225 text; the Council of Europe copy on coe.int is the treaty's own authoritative version and was not fetched). TEXT SAYS: Art. 15(2) is the interaction-notification duty and Art. 8 names "identification of content generated by artificial intelligence systems". TEXT SAYS, with one correction to the claim's wording: Art. 15(2) reads "shall seek to ensure ... as appropriate for the context" — a best-efforts obligation qualified by context, not "shall ensure"; Art. 15(1), by contrast, uses "shall ensure". The claim's phrase "asks Parties to ensure" overstates the strength slightly and should read "asks Parties to seek to ensure, as appropriate for the context". REASONABLE READING: neither Art. 8 nor Art. 15 contains any wording about identifying the operator, deployer, owner or natural person behind an AI system or agent; both speak only of the system and its content. This is an absence claim checked against the verbatim text of those two articles only; I did not scan every other article of the Convention for an identification-of-operator duty, so the negative limb is scoped to Art. 8 and Art. 15 as the claim states it. Not a legal determination.

verdicts.claim: Under the revised Swiss FADP a controller must inform data subjects of its identity and contact details when collecting personal data (Art. 19(2)(a)), with a fine of up to CHF 250,000 on complaint for wilful failure (Art. 60(1)).
verdicts.evidence_quote: Art. 19 Duty to provide information when collecting personal data — 1 The controller shall inform the data subject in an appropriate manner when collecting personal data; this duty to provide information also applies if the data is not collected from the data subject. 2 It shall provide the data subject on collecting the data with the information required for the data subject to exercise their rights under this Act and to guarantee transparent data processing; it shall provide the following information as a minimum: a. the controller's identity and contact details; b. the purpose of processing; c. if applicable, the recipients or the categories of recipients to which personal data is disclosed.
